title: Fixed-size window
sub: Add the one coming in, subtract the one leaving: from O(n·k) to O(n), plus an FPS counter on a ring buffer
cards/0/title: The problem and the window signals
cards/0/body:
Maximum Average Subarray I (LeetCode #643). Given an integer array nums and a number k, find the contiguous subarray of length exactly k with the largest average and return that average. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴.

Signals of a sliding window:

1. The problem is about a contiguous piece: “subarray”, “substring”, “k in a row”, “the last N frames”. A subsequence — elements with gaps — is no longer a window.
2. You need the best piece or an answer for every position of the piece: the largest sum, the longest, the shortest.
3. Whatever you compute over the piece can be updated when one element enters on the right and one leaves on the left: a sum, a count, letter counters.

Here the length is given, so this is a fixed-size window: the left edge follows the right one at exactly distance k. The average is the sum divided by k, and k is the same for every window. So it is enough to find the largest sum and divide once at the end.
cards/1/q: Where does a fixed-size window work? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: The largest sum of k consecutive elements
cards/1/options/1: Does string s contain a substring of length |p| made of the same letters as p
cards/1/options/2: The average frame time over the last 60 frames, updated every frame
cards/1/options/3: The largest sum of any k elements of the array, not necessarily consecutive
cards/1/explain: A sum of k in a row is the template itself. A permutation of p inside s is a window of length |p| with letter counters: a letter enters — plus one, a letter leaves — minus one. The last 60 frames is a window over a stream of values. Any k elements with gaps is not a window: you need the k largest, not a piece — that is sorting or a heap. A subsequence has gaps too, so no window.
cards/2/title: The naive solution and its cost
cards/2/body:
Brute force: for every start i from 0 to n − k, add up k elements from scratch. There are n − k + 1 windows with k additions each — (n − k + 1)·k in total, that is O(n·k) time and O(1) memory.

The cost depends on k. With k = 1 there are n windows, but one addition each. With k = n there is one window, but of length n. The middle is the worst: with k ≈ n/2 the work is ≈ n²/4. For n = 10⁵ that is 2.5·10⁹ additions — at the rule of thumb of 10⁸ simple operations per second, about 25 seconds instead of a fraction of a second.

So O(n·k) must not be called “almost linear”: when k is comparable to n, it is a square.
cards/3/q: n = 10⁵. For which k does the naive solution do the most additions?
cards/3/explain: The work is (n − k + 1)·k: the number of windows times the window length. For k = 1 it is n, for k = n it is n as well. The factors always add up to n + 1, and a product of two numbers with a fixed sum peaks when they are equal: k ≈ n/2 gives ≈ n²/4 = 2.5·10⁹.
cards/3/wrong/0: With k = 1 there are n windows, but one addition each — n in total.
cards/3/wrong/2: With k = n there is a single window: n additions. A long window, but only one.
cards/4/body:
Neighbouring windows [i..i+k−1] and [i+1..i+k] share k − 1 elements. The naive solution adds them up again. Yet the windows differ in just two elements: nums[r] entered on the right and nums[r − k] left on the left.

So we don’t recompute the sum, we patch it: sum += nums[r] − nums[r − k]. One step is O(1), the whole pass is O(n), memory O(1).

Invariant: after the slide at step r, sum holds the sum of exactly the last k elements, nums[r − k + 1..r]. The element that leaves has index r − k — the one k positions to the left of the incoming one.

No overflow: |sum| ≤ k·10⁴ ≤ 10⁹, and int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹. Compare sums and divide once, at the end, and make sure it is in double.

In a game: the same window smooths noisy input — the average of the last k samples of a stick, a mouse or an accelerometer.
cards/5/explain: The starting window is the first k elements, and best starts from its sum, not from zero: if every number is negative, zero beats every window and the answer is wrong. The leaving element is nums[r − k], k positions left of the incoming one; r − k + 1 is the first element that stays. best / k is integer division: 51 / 4 gives 12, not 12.75, so cast to double before dividing.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [3, 8, 2, 6, 1, 9, 4, 7], k = 3. The rig stops twice: first it asks which element leaves the window, then what the method returns.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: Window [8, 2, 6], sum = 16. nums[4] = 1 comes in. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The leaving element is nums[r − k] = nums[1] = 8, the leftmost element of the current window. The 3 already left on the previous step, and the 2 stays: the new window is [2, 6, 1] with sum 9. best stays 16.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The best sum is 20, for the window [9, 4, 7]. What does return (double)best / k return?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The cast to double comes before the division, so 20.0 is divided by 3: the answer is 6.666…. Without the cast, best / k is integer division and gives 6. And 20 is the sum, not the average.
cards/7/title: Unity: an FPS counter on a ring buffer
cards/7/body:
FPS shown as 1 / Time.deltaTime jumps every frame. What you want on screen is the average over the last N frames — a fixed-size window, except the numbers arrive as a stream, and there is no point in keeping the whole history.

Keep the last N values in an array plus an index head — the slot of the oldest value. Every frame: subtract the leaving frames[head], add the new value, write the new value in its place and move head around the circle. That is a ring buffer: O(1) per frame and zero allocations. A Queue<float> would also do — internally it is the same circular array — but your own array is clearer and never grows.

Details you will be asked about:
— Use Time.unscaledDeltaTime. Time.deltaTime is multiplied by Time.timeScale — on a pause with timeScale = 0 it is zero — and capped by Time.maximumDeltaTime.
— Average FPS is N / the sum of frame times, not the average of 1/dt. Frames of 10 and 30 ms: the average of 100 and 33.3 FPS is 66.7, but in fact 2 frames took 40 ms, which is 50 FPS. Averaging instantaneous FPS is skewed upward by the fast frames.
— Until the buffer is full, divide by the number of frames recorded, not by N.
— A float accumulates rounding error over millions of additions and subtractions, and the sum slowly drifts. Recompute it every N frames or keep it in a double.

Ring buffers in detail, with mask indexing, come in the last unit of the course, in the lesson on pools and ring buffers.
cards/8/q: In this counter the sum stays zero forever. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/8/explain: The new value is written into the slot before the old one is subtracted from the sum. The next line then subtracts not the leaving frame but the one just written: sum += dt − dt, and the sum never changes. As with check-before-insert in Two Sum, order matters: first sum += dt − frames[head], then frames[head] = dt.
cards/9/q: An FPS counter on a window of N frames. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: A counter on Time.deltaTime gets zero-length frames during a pause with Time.timeScale = 0
cards/9/options/1: Two frames of 10 and 30 ms make 50 FPS, not 66.7
cards/9/options/2: The average of instantaneous 1/dt is more accurate than N / the sum of frame times
cards/9/options/3: Every frame the counter allocates memory for the new value
cards/9/options/4: A float sum drifts slowly over millions of additions and subtractions
cards/9/explain: deltaTime is multiplied by timeScale, so on a pause it is zero — use unscaledDeltaTime. Two frames in 40 ms are 2 / 0.04 = 50 FPS, while the average of 100 and 33.3 is inflated by the fast frame. There are no allocations: the array is allocated once and one slot is overwritten per frame. float rounding error accumulates, which is why the sum is recomputed now and then or kept in a double.
cards/10/title: Which quantities work this way — and which don’t
cards/10/body:
The “add the incoming, subtract the leaving” trick works when adding an element can be undone:

— sum and average: subtract;
— the number of matching elements (vowels, enemies in a zone, zeros): −1 if a matching one left;
— letter counters int[26]: count[in]++, count[out]--;
— XOR: XOR-ing again removes the element.

It does not work for the maximum and minimum. Window [9, 4, 7], maximum 9; the 9 leaves — what is the maximum now? A single number “9” cannot tell you; you need to remember who the next candidate is. That is the sliding window maximum problem, and a monotonic deque solves it — lesson 4 of this unit.

A window can also be written as a single loop: an element always enters, one leaves once r ≥ k, and the answer is taken once the window has reached length k.
cards/10/deep:
Prefix sums as an alternative. prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements, so the sum of window [l..r] is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]. That costs O(n) memory instead of O(1), but answers the sum of any range in O(1): handy when there are many window lengths or the queries arrive after the precomputation. Keep prefixes in long: with n = 10⁵ and |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴ the sum reaches 10⁹, and with larger values it overflows int.

Rolling hash (Rabin–Karp, substring search). The polynomial hash of a window, h = Σ s[i]·B^(k−1−i) mod M, also slides in O(1): subtract the leaving character’s contribution s[l]·B^(k−1), multiply by B, add the incoming one. Searching for a pattern of length m in a text of length n is O(n + m) on average. Equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings, so a match is verified character by character, and in the worst case with collisions it is O(n·m).

Precision. The drift of a float sum is the accumulated rounding error of every +=; float carries about 7 significant digits. The fixes are recomputing every N steps, summing in double, or Kahan compensated summation (a second variable collects the lost low-order bits). Integers do not drift — which is why frame times are sometimes stored as microseconds in a long.

Unity. unscaledDeltaTime is the full interval between frames, including waiting for vsync or the GPU. To see who is slow, the CPU or the GPU, there is FrameTimingManager (CPU and GPU time per frame) and ProfilerRecorder (profiler counters in a build); an averaging window over their numbers is built the same way.
cards/11/q: You are solving Maximum Average Subarray I out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: length exactly k, can numbers be negative, return a double, n and k up to 10⁵
cards/11/items/1: Name the brute force: (n − k + 1)·k additions, up to 2.5·10⁹ with k ≈ n/2
cards/11/items/2: Idea: neighbouring windows share k − 1 elements — add the incoming, subtract the leaving
cards/11/items/3: Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: sum holds exactly the last k elements
cards/11/items/4: Run the example [1, 12, −5, −6, 50, 3], k = 4 — the answer is 12.75
cards/11/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: k = n, every number negative, division in double
cards/11/explain: As with any problem: agree on the statement, name the baseline and its cost, then the idea, the code and a run on an example, and only then the complexity and edge cases. “Every number negative” checks that best starts from the first sum, not from zero.
cards/12/q: Match each window quantity with how to update it on a slide.
cards/12/pairs/1/1: +1 if a vowel entered; −1 if one left
cards/12/pairs/3/1: Keep the sum, divide once at the end
cards/12/pairs/4/1: Cannot be undone by subtraction: needs a deque
